nodes.title: Clean plate matting
widgets_values:
CLEAN PLATE MATTING - alpha from ONE take and ONE clean plate

Shoot the subject, take the subject away, shoot the empty set. That is the whole capture. The classic objection is that a single pair cannot give an exact alpha, because C = a F + (1-a) B is three equations in four unknowns - and that is true PER PIXEL. Over a WINDOW in which alpha and the foreground colour are roughly constant it is a regression of the take on the plate:

    C_i = (1-a) B_i + a F      ->     slope = 1 - a,   intercept = a F

and the slope is identifiable as soon as the BACKGROUND VARIES inside the window. The backdrop's own texture plays the part of Smith & Blinn's second backdrop. 'CV Local Linear Fit' computes exactly that, and it is exact on flat-alpha regions: opaque subject, clean background, and - the interesting one - the uniformly translucent glass panel, which no amount of colour propagation could ever guess (0.44 recovered against a truth of 0.42).

Where alpha varies inside the window (every soft edge, every hair) the regression is smeared, so 'CV Clean Plate Matte' keeps only the foreground COLOUR from it - from the pixels that are BOTH confidently inside the subject AND locally flat, eroded by another 6 px - propagates that colour into the edges with cv2.inpaint, and re-solves alpha per pixel:

    a = <C - B, F - B> / |F - B|^2

TWO VARIANTS, same solver.

1. THE IDEAL PAIR (top). The plate is literally the background pixels of the take, so C - B is EXACTLY zero outside the subject - and alpha is a dot product with C - B, so it comes out EXACTLY 0 at 100% of the pixels where the two frames are byte-identical (69% of this frame). Not 'almost'. Mean |alpha - truth| over the whole frame: 0.0027, and the worst pixel the subject does not touch at all is 0.014 - which is the subject's own sub-quantization fringe, not a leak. Nothing here is suppressed, cleaned or filtered; there is nothing to clean.

2. THE REAL PAIR (middle). Same subject, but the tripod was nudged and the lamps drifted between the two exposures, and both frames carry sensor noise. 'Plate Align (Geometric + Photometric)' fixes the geometry with a RANSAC homography and the light with a trimmed per-channel gain/bias fit - neither stage needs to know where the subject is, because the subject is an OUTLIER of both models. What is left is a low, frame-wide alpha haze, which 'Matte Cleanup' removes:

    raw plate                      0.148    79% of the background above 0.02
    photometric correction only    0.093    43%
    geometric registration only    0.098    90%
    aligned, no cleanup            0.0147   24%
    aligned + cleanup              0.0059    0.3%, worst pixel 0.10

The cleanup's four stages each kill a DIFFERENT statistic, which is why the mean error alone hides them: the coverage gate removes the strip the warp could not fill (worst pixel 1.00 -> 0.54), the dead zone removes the haze (mean 0.0135 -> 0.0002), the morphological open removes the isolated survivors (0.12% -> 0.03% of the background) and the guided filter halves the worst pixel again (0.31 -> 0.10) while snapping what remains onto the take's own edges. Run the same cleanup on variant 1 and it only does damage (0.0027 -> 0.0062) - it is a fix for a misaligned plate, not a default.

The bottom row runs the identical solver on the RAW plate, with no alignment and no cleanup, so the difference is visible on the canvas rather than only in this note.

WHEN THIS FAILS: a FLAT backdrop. The regression needs the background to vary inside the window - check the 'plate_texture' output, which is the local standard deviation of the plate in gray levels (about 11 here). Against a plain wall or a lit screen the opaque parts and the edges still come out (they only need F to differ from B), but a uniformly translucent region is genuinely unrecoverable from one pair - that is the case for the 'CV Triangulation Matte' blueprint, which solves it exactly from a SECOND backdrop at the cost of needing the subject to hold still across two takes.

SHOOTING NOTES: lock exposure, focus and white balance; prefer a backdrop with fine, non-repeating texture over a clean sweep; keep the subject far enough from the backdrop that it is not lit by bounce; and shoot the plate immediately after the take, on the same tripod.
